questions.expected_answer: The clinical study period was January 2021 to January 2022. Eligible patients were adults 18 years or older with documented Bethesda score after FNA; no prior sonography or an ultrasound-to-FNA interval greater than two weeks was excluded. Overall TI-RADS kappa 0.504 (95% CI 0.409–0.599). The later data-access period is not the clinical study period.
questions.query: For the sonographer-versus-radiologist thyroid TI-RADS agreement study, what clinical study period and age/biopsy-timing eligibility rules defined the cohort, and what overall TI-RADS kappa with confidence interval was reported?

support_sets.quote: The study employed a retrospective design, covering the period from January 2021 to January 2022.

The patients were considered eligible if they were an adult (18 years or older) and had a documented Bethesda score following an FNA biopsy done after the ultrasound scan. Patients who did not undergo thyroid sonography prior to the FNA or the duration between the scan and FNA was more than two weeks were excluded.

The study employed a retrospective design, covering the period from January 2021 to January 2022.

The patients were considered eligible if they were an adult (18 years or older) and had a documented Bethesda score following an FNA biopsy done after the ultrasound scan. Patients who did not undergo thyroid sonography prior to the FNA or the duration between the scan and FNA was more than two weeks were excluded.

The study revealed a moderate overall agreement between sonographers and radiologists in TI-RADS scoring (κ = 0.504; 95% CI: 0.409–0.599), with poor agreement noted specifically for nodule margin scores (κ = 0.102; 95% CI: -1.430–0.301).

questions.query: In the sonographer-versus-radiologist thyroid TI-RADS study, what training materials and period of monitoring and feedback followed the sonographers’ focused course, and what margin-score kappa, confidence interval and p-value were reported?

support_sets.quote: All sonographers were trained to interpret thyroid US images and assign ACR TI-RADS scores after receiving a focused training course by the chief consultant radiologist (12 years of experience). The training was done in July 2020, which included official educational materials developed by the ACR including the TI-RADS atlas and user guide [32]. This was followed by regular monitoring and feedback over 3 months.

All sonographers were trained to interpret thyroid US images and assign ACR TI-RADS scores after receiving a focused training course by the chief consultant radiologist (12 years of experience). The training was done in July 2020, which included official educational materials developed by the ACR including the TI-RADS atlas and user guide [32]. This was followed by regular monitoring and feedback over 3 months.

The study revealed a moderate overall agreement between sonographers and radiologists in TI-RADS scoring (κ = 0.504; 95% CI: 0.409–0.599), with poor agreement noted specifically for nodule margin scores (κ = 0.102; 95% CI: -1.430–0.301).
The margin score, however, was not significant (p = 0.153) and the Kappa statistic of 0.102 indicated slight agreement.

components.query: In the sonographer-versus-radiologist thyroid TI-RADS diagnostic-accuracy analysis, which Bethesda categories were excluded as indeterminate?
In the sonographer-versus-radiologist thyroid TI-RADS diagnostic-accuracy analysis, what sensitivity and specificity with confidence intervals were reported for each reader group?

questions.expected_answer: Indeterminate Bethesda I, III and IV were excluded. Sonographer sensitivity 100.0% (95% CI 71.5–100.0), specificity 44.6% (34.2–53.3); radiologist sensitivity 100.0% (71.5–100.0), specificity 29.3% (20.3–39.8). These are the source-reported diagnostic estimates; the source’s threshold and pathology terminology discrepancies are retained separately.

The indeterminate (Bethesda I, III, and IV) scores were excluded from the diagnostic accuracy analysis.

The sonographers achieved a sensitivity of 100% (95% CI: 71.5–100.0), indicating accurate identification of all positive (suspicious or malignant) cases (11 out of 11). However, specificity was moderate at 44.6% (95% CI: 34.2–53.3), suggesting a higher rate of false-positive diagnoses compared to true negatives.

Similarly, the radiologist’s sensitivity was 100% (95% CI: 71.5–100.0). However, specificity was lower at 29.3% (95% CI: 20.3–39.8), indicating a greater tendency for false positives with only 27 of 92 non-malignant cases correctly identified.

components.query: In the COPCOV trial, what ordered laboratory-confirmation hierarchy and fallback conditions defined symptomatic laboratory-confirmed COVID-19?
In the COPCOV trial’s primary intention-to-treat symptomatic COVID-19 analysis, how were missing outcomes handled?
In the COPCOV trial’s overall primary symptomatic COVID-19 comparison of hydroxychloroquine/chloroquine against placebo, what risk ratio with confidence interval was reported?

questions.expected_answer: The hierarchy was positive nose/throat swab PCR; if PCR was negative, failed or not done, paired baseline/end-study serum seroconversion; only if paired sera were unavailable or uninterpretable, adapted dried-blood-spot seroconversion. Missing primary ITT outcomes were treated as no COVID-19 during the study period. Overall trial RR 0.85 (95% CI 0.72–1.00), distinct from PCR-only RR and the prespecified meta-analysis.
questions.query: In the COPCOV trial’s primary symptomatic COVID-19 analysis, what ordered laboratory-confirmation hierarchy was used, how were missing outcomes handled in intention-to-treat analysis, and what overall treatment-versus-placebo risk ratio with confidence interval was reported?

support_sets.quote: The primary outcome was symptomatic laboratory-confirmed COVID-19 defined as symptoms consistent with COVID-19 and laboratory evidence of SARS-CoV-2 infection (S1 Appendix). Laboratory evidence was defined by a prespecified hierarchy: first by a nose and/or throat swab PCR positive for SARS-CoV-2; second, if the PCR was negative, failed, or not done, by seroconversion (S-protein IgG antibody) based on baseline and end of study paired sera [28]; and third, only if paired sera were unavailable or uninterpretable, by seroconversion from the contingency DBS in an adapted assay. The prespecified primary endpoint determination algorithm code is provided in the GitHub repository.

components.query: In the COPCOV trial, what loading and daily maintenance dose regimen and duration were assigned for hydroxychloroquine or chloroquine prophylaxis?
In the COPCOV trial, what model analysed participant-reported lost workdays?
In the COPCOV trial, what arm-specific mean workdays lost per participants and between-arm mean difference with confidence intervals were reported?

questions.expected_answer: A loading dose of 10 mg base/kg was followed by 155 mg base daily for 3 months, equivalent to 250 mg chloroquine phosphate or 200 mg hydroxychloroquine sulphate daily. A zero-inflated Poisson model gave over 90 days 337 workdays lost (95% CI 279–398) per 1,000 HCQ/CQ participants and 441 (370–515) per 1,000 placebo participants, mean difference 104 days (12–199).
questions.query: In the COPCOV trial, what loading and daily maintenance regimen and duration were assigned, what model analysed lost workdays, and what arm-specific mean workdays lost and between-arm mean difference with confidence intervals were reported?

support_sets.quote: A loading dose of 10 mg base/kg (four 155 mg tablets for a 60 kg subject) was followed by 155 mg daily (equivalent to 250 mg chloroquine phosphate or 200 mg hydroxychloroquine sulphate) for 3 months.

Under a zero-inflated Poisson regression model, the mean number of workdays lost over 90 days of chemoprophylaxis was 337 (95% CI, 279 to 398) per 1,000 participants in HCQ/CQ recipients and 441 (95% CI, 370 to 515) per 1,000 in placebo recipients; a mean difference of 104 days (95% CI, 12 to 199).

questions.expected_answer: Asymptomatic laboratory-confirmed SARS-CoV-2 infection was a prespecified secondary outcome. Events were 267/2,320 HCQ/CQ recipients and 280/2,332 placebo recipients, RR 0.96 (95% CI 0.82–1.12). These are asymptomatic events, distinct from symptomatic infection and all-infection combined totals.

support_sets.quote: There were 3 prespecified secondary outcomes: asymptomatic laboratory-confirmed SARS-CoV-2 infection; severity of COVID-19 symptoms; and all-cause PCR-confirmed symptomatic acute respiratory illness (including SARS-CoV-2 infection).

Asymptomatic COVID-19 occurred in 267/2,320 (11.5% [95% CI, 10.2 to 12.9]), HCQ/CQ recipients and 280/2,332 (12.0% [95% CI, 10.7 to 13.4]) placebo recipients (RR: 0.96 [95% CI, 0.82 to 1.12; p = 0.6]).

There were 3 prespecified secondary outcomes: asymptomatic laboratory-confirmed SARS-CoV-2 infection; severity of COVID-19 symptoms; and all-cause PCR-confirmed symptomatic acute respiratory illness (including SARS-CoV-2 infection).

components.query: In the COPCOV trial, what incremental costs and quality-adjusted life-year gains were measured for hydroxychloroquine/chloroquine prophylaxis?
In the COPCOV trial, what incremental cost-effectiveness ratio was reported for hydroxychloroquine/chloroquine prophylaxis?

context_anchors.quote: There were 3 generic prespecified trial tertiary outcomes: the participant reported number of workdays lost; genetic and baseline biochemical markers associated with symptomatic COVID-19, respiratory illness, and disease severity (not reported here); and health economic analyses of HCQ and CQ prophylaxis on costs and quality of life measures (not reported here).
A health economic analysis will be reported separately.

questions.null_reason: Health economic analysis was a planned tertiary outcome explicitly not reported in this main article and stated to be reported separately. Workdays lost and claims of inexpensive drugs are context, not measured incremental cost/QALY results or an ICER.
